observations.content:
Summary: PEP 703, authored by Sam Gross and sponsored by Łukasz Langa, proposes to make the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) optional in CPython. The PEP adds a build configuration flag `--disable-gil` to the configure script, allowing for a build of CPython without the GIL. The GIL will remain the default for CPython builds and python.org downloads. The PEP was finalized on October 24, 2023, and is intended for Python 3.13. The proposal has been accepted and discussed on multiple platforms, including Hacker News and the Python Steering Council.

Summary: PEP 703 proposes adding a build configuration to CPython to run Python code without the global interpreter lock (GIL) and make the interpreter thread-safe. PEP 779 outlines three phases of development for removing the GIL, with the free-threaded build becoming officially supported but still optional in phase II. PEP 805 discusses the need for a generalization of the GIL to allow parallel execution, highlighting the risks of race conditions in the current GIL-less approach. The sources do not provide a definitive timeline for when these phases will be completed.

[1] PEP 703 – Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython | peps.python.org
    https://peps.python.org/pep-0703
    See PEP 1 for how to propose changes.

## Abstract

CPython’s global interpreter lock (“GIL”) prevents multiple threads from executing Python code at the same time. The GIL is an obstacle to using multi-core CPUs from Python efficiently. This PEP proposes adding a build configuration (`--disable-gil`) to CPython to let it run Python code without the global interpreter lock and with the necessary changes needed to make the interpreter thread-safe.

## Motivation [...] This PEP proposes a new API `PyDict_FetchItem` which behaves like `PyDict_GetItem`, but returns a new reference instead of a borrowed reference. As described in Borrowed References, some uses of borrowed references that were safe when running with the GIL are unsafe when running without the GIL and need to be replaced by functions like `PyDict_FetchItem` that return new references. [...] The GIL is a CPython implementation detail that limits multithreaded parallelism, so it might seem unintuitive to think of it as a usability issue. However, library authors frequently care a great deal about performance and will design APIs that support working around the GIL. These workaround frequently lead to APIs that are more difficult to use. Consequently, users of these APIs may experience the GIL as a usability issue and not just a performance issue.

Summary: PEP 703 proposes adding a build configuration to CPython to run Python code without the global interpreter lock (GIL), making it optional. The GIL will remain the default for CPython builds and python.org downloads, but a new build configuration flag, `--disable-gil`, will enable a free-threaded Python interpreter. The PEP aims to improve Python's efficiency on multi-core CPUs by allowing multiple threads to execute Python code simultaneously. The PEP is final and targeted for Python 3.13, with discussions and updates ongoing.

Summary: PEP 703 proposes making the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) optional in CPython by adding a build configuration that removes the GIL, resulting in a free-threaded Python interpreter. This was formally accepted in October 2023 and is set to be officially supported in Python 3.14 under PEP 779. The no-GIL build is not ABI-compatible with the standard build, requiring C extensions to be rebuilt. The new build flag is `--disable-gil`, and the free-threaded build will have a separate ABI tag carrying a `t` suffix.

# What is PEP 703?

by Tim Hopper ·  Markdown

PEP 703: Making the Global Interpreter Lock Optional in CPython is the proposal that makes a no-GIL CPython build real. It adds a build configuration that removes the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL), the mutex that lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time, producing the free-threaded Python interpreter. [...] CPython gains a build flag, `--disable-gil`, that compiles an interpreter without the GIL. Because removing the lock changes the Python object header (to support biased reference counting), the free-threaded build is not ABI-compatible with the standard build. C extensions must be rebuilt, and wheels are published under a separate ABI tag carrying a `t` suffix. [...] The PEP was authored by Sam Gross at Meta. The Steering Council announced intent to accept in July 2023 and formally accepted the PEP on 24 October 2023 with a phased rollout: experimental in 3.13, officially supported under PEP 779: Criteria for supported status for free-threaded Python in 3.14, with any default-build switch deferred for years.
